title: The Learning Science of Deep Processing
author: Kognitivo
summary: Kognitivo's argument rests on a distinction between levels of processing: surface processing (cramming, rereading, highlight) is effort that feels productive but produces shallow, fragile memory; deep processing (elaborating, connecting, explaining to someone else, teaching) requires more effort upfront but produces durable understanding that transfers. The research is clear: students who engage in deep processing learn faster and remember longer, yet most students default to surface processing because it feels easier and more comfortable. The teaching move is to push students toward deep processing through deliberate structures: explanation to a peer, elaboration questions (why does this matter? how does this connect to what you already know?), teaching a simplified version to someone else, generating examples. The piece is not novel in its findings (the research is settled) but useful in its emphasis on the gap between what feels productive and what actually works. Most classroom work defaulting to surface-processing activities (reading, highlighting, listening, taking notes) leaves the heavy lifting of deep processing to the student's free time and motivation.
points: Surface processing (cramming, rereading, highlighting) feels productive but produces shallow, fragile memory; deep processing requires more effort but produces durable understanding that transfers.
Students default to surface processing because it feels easier and more comfortable, yet research is clear that deep processing produces faster learning and longer retention.
Teaching must push students toward deep processing through deliberate structures: explanation to peers, elaboration questions, teaching simplified versions, generating examples.
quotes: Shallow processing involves focusing on attributes that remain on the surface or the look-alike of what you want to learn (typically at the visual or sound levels), such as the appearance or pronunciation of words. It also refers to engaging in rote activities that reinforce those superficial aspects like repetition, rereading and highlighting.

Concentration is about attention. It's the ability to sustain focus and resist distraction. Deep processing is about what you do with that focus. You can concentrate intensely on a shallow task. Anyone who has ever memorized a list word for word knows this feeling. It takes effort. It feels demanding. And yet the information often disappears quickly.

A recent study showed that simply asking students “why?” after introducing new information made them remember that information incredibly better. The reason is elaborative interrogation: studies show that students who generate explanations remember more and transfer knowledge better than those who simply read explanations.

Research shows that relating information to yourself provides a powerful scaffold to organize information, not just emotional relevance. In practice, this means that tying information to personal experiences, goals or beliefs helps encoding by making it feel relevant to one's own life.

Short learning bursts feel faster, but they can slow down the path to durable understanding when they prevent deep engagement. Ironically, learners often reach long-term retention sooner by spending time processing meaning deeply than by spreading attention thin across many brief sessions.

Efficiency in learning is not necessarily about shorter exposure. It's about doing the right kind of thinking for the right amount of time and, paradoxically, that often means “for long enough”.” Archived from Kognitivo on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
